q: A plant disease is usually defined as abnormal ____ and/or dysfunction of a plant.
e: Plant diseases involve abnormal growth or dysfunction resulting from a disturbance in the plant's normal life processes.

q: Diseases are the result of some disturbance in the normal ____ process of the plant.
e: Any disruption to the normal life processes of a plant can lead to the development of a disease.

q: Diseases may be the result of living and/or ____ causes.
e: Plant diseases can originate from biotic (living) pathogens or abiotic (non-living) environmental factors.

q: Biotic diseases are caused by ____ organisms (e.g., fungi, bacteria, and viruses).
e: Biotic agents are living pathogens capable of infecting a host and reproducing.

q: Abiotic diseases are caused by non-living ____ conditions (e.g., soil compaction, wind, frost, soil salt damage, and girdling roots).
e: Abiotic diseases arise from unfavorable environmental or physical conditions rather than infectious agents.

q: Plant disease is any abnormal condition that alters the appearance or ____ of a plant.
e: Diseases manifest through visible changes in appearance or disruptions in the plant's physiological functions.

q: Most plant diseases, around ____ percent are caused by fungal or fungal-like organisms.
e: Fungi and fungal-like organisms are responsible for the vast majority of known plant diseases.

q: However, other serious diseases of food and feed crops are caused by ____ and bacterial organisms.
e: Along with bacteria, viruses are major causal agents of serious crop diseases.

q: Certain ____ also cause plant diseases.
e: Nematodes are microscopic roundworms that act as plant parasites and can cause significant disease.

q: Nematodes are very tiny ____.
e: Nematodes belong to a group of simple, unsegmented roundworms.

q: They are plant parasites and help distribute bacteria and fungi through the soil as well as along ____.
e: Nematode activity in the soil and along root systems can facilitate the spread of other pathogens.

q: Some plant diseases are classified as "____," or diseases that are non-infectious and include damage from air pollution, nutritional deficiencies or toxicities.
e: Abiotic diseases are non-infectious disorders caused by environmental stressors rather than living pathogens.

q: Infectious plant diseases are caused by a ____ organism such as a fungus, bacterium, mycoplasma, virus, viroid, nematode, or parasitic flowering plant.
e: A pathogenic organism is one that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.

q: An infectious agent is capable of ____ within or on its host and spreading from one susceptible host to another.
e: The ability to reproduce within a host is a defining characteristic of infectious pathogens.

q: Non-infectious plant diseases are caused by ____ growing conditions, including extremes of temperature.
e: Environmental stress and unfavourable growing conditions trigger non-infectious plant disorders.

q: Because non-infectious causal agents are not organisms capable of reproducing within a host, they are not ____.
e: Unlike biotic pathogens, abiotic factors cannot spread or be transmitted from one plant to another.

q: The study of plant diseases is called plant ____.
e: Plant pathology is the scientific study of diseases in plants and their causal agents.

q: Pathology is derived from the two Greek words pathos (suffering, disease) and ____ (discourse, study).
e: The term pathology combines the Greek words for suffering (pathos) and study (logos).

q: Plant pathology thus means a study of plant ____.
e: By definition, plant pathology focuses entirely on understanding and managing plant diseases.

q: Plant disease is caused by a pathogen (biotic or infectious disease) or an ____ factor (abiotic or non-infectious disease).
e: The two primary categories of disease-causing factors are biological pathogens and environmental stressors.

q: Biotic diseases can spread throughout one plant and also may spread to ____ plants of the same species.
e: Infectious diseases have the capacity to move from an infected plant to nearby susceptible plants.

q: Biotic diseases sometimes show physical evidence (signs) of the pathogen, such as fungal growth, bacterial ____, or nematode cysts.
e: Bacterial ooze is a common physical sign indicating the presence of a bacterial infection in plant tissue.

q: Many plant problems, especially biotic problems, if not recognized and controlled early in their development, they can result in significant ____ damage for the producer.
e: Uncontrolled plant diseases can lead to severe crop losses and substantial economic damage for farmers.

q: Therefore, timely and accurate ____ are required so that appropriate pest and disease management options can be implemented.
e: Proper identification and diagnosis are critical first steps in implementing effective disease control measures.

q: Abiotic diseases are caused by nonliving factors, such as drought stress, sunscald, freeze injury, wind injury, chemical injury, nutrient ____, or improper cultural practices.
e: A lack of essential nutrients in the soil can cause abiotic disorders known as nutrient deficiencies.

q: Abiotic damage often occurs on many plant ____.
e: Environmental stressors like drought or chemical drift typically affect a wide variety of plant species simultaneously.

q: In contrast, biotic disease problems are more limited to a certain ____.
e: Pathogens are often highly specific and will only infect particular host species or cultivars.

q: For example, the fungi that cause tomato leaf blight do not cause damage on sweet ____.
e: Host specificity means a pathogen affecting tomatoes will not necessarily infect unrelated crops like sweet corn.

q: Abiotic damage does not ____ from plant to plant over time.
e: Because they are not caused by reproducing organisms, abiotic disorders do not spread contagiously.

q: Abiotic diseases do not show the presence of disease ____.
e: Unlike biotic diseases, abiotic disorders lack physical signs like fungal fruiting bodies or bacterial ooze.

q: Plant diseases occurrence and severity result from the impact of three factors: the host plant, the pathogen and the ____ conditions.
e: The disease triangle illustrates that disease requires a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen, and favorable environmental conditions.

q: This is represented with the disease ____ as shown in Figure 4.2.
e: The disease triangle is a fundamental concept in plant pathology depicting the three interacting factors required for disease.

q: Signs of plant disease are physical ____ of the pathogen.
e: Signs refer to the observable physical presence of the pathogen itself or its byproducts.

q: Signs can also help with plant disease ____.
e: Observing specific signs, such as spore masses, is crucial for accurately identifying the causal pathogen.

q: Signs are the actual ____ causing the disease.
e: Signs represent the physical structures of the living organisms responsible for the infection.

q: Signs include conks, fruiting bodies, mildew, mushrooms, mycelium, rhizomorphs, slime flux or ooze, spore masses, insects and/or their ____.
e: Frass, or insect excrement, is considered a sign of insect presence and potential vectoring of disease.

q: ____ are visible effects of disease on plants.
e: Symptoms are the host plant's visible physiological reactions to a pathogen or environmental stressor.

q: Any detectable changes in colour, shape, and/or functions of the plant in response to a pathogen or disease-causing agent is a ____.
e: A symptom reflects the altered appearance or function of the plant due to the disease process.

q: Symptoms of disease are the plant's ____ to the causal agent.
e: Symptoms manifest as the host plant's biological reaction to the presence of a pathogen.

q: Plant symptoms include blight, canker, chlorosis, decline, dieback, distortion, gall or gall-like, gummosis, leaf distortion, leaf scorch, leaf spot, mosaic, necrosis, stunting, wilt, witches' broom, insect feeding ____.
e: Insect feeding injury is a visible symptom that can also predispose the plant to secondary pathogenic infections.

q: Viruses cause mottling, spots, mosaic-like patterns, crinkling, and other malformations on leaves and ____.
e: Viral infections frequently manifest as distinct color patterns and malformations on both foliage and developing fruits.

q: Because viruses are ____, infected plants must be rogued or discarded.
e: Systemic viruses spread throughout the entire plant vascular system, making localized treatment impossible and requiring removal.

q: Common virus diseases in plants include curly top virus in tomatoes, cucumber ____ virus in tomatoes and vine crops.
e: Cucumber mosaic virus is a widespread pathogen affecting a broad range of vegetable and vine crops.

q: Fungi and fungal-like organisms (FLOs) cause more plant diseases than any other group of plant pest with over ____ species shown to cause disease.
e: Fungi represent the largest and most diverse group of plant pathogens, with thousands of species capable causing disease.

q: FLOs are organisms like Pythium and Phytophthora and cause downy ____.
e: Fungal-like organisms such as Phytophthora are notorious for causing devastating downy mildew and root rot diseases.

q: Most pathogenic fungi belong to the following genera: Alternaria, Aspergillus, Botrytis, Fusarium, Puccinia, Rhizopus, and ____.
e: Sclerotinia is a major fungal genus known for causing soft rot and white mold in various crops.

q: Alternaria causes leaf spots and ____ of various plants.
e: Alternaria species are common pathogens responsible for leaf spot diseases and blights across many plant families.

q: Aspergillus causes rots of ____.
e: Aspergillus fungi frequently infect and cause storage rots in harvested seeds and grains.

q: Puccinia causes ____ of cereals.
e: Puccinia is the primary genus of fungi responsible for devastating rust diseases in cereal crops like wheat.

q: Rhizopus causes soft rot of ____.
e: Rhizopus stolonifer is a common post-harvest pathogen that causes rapid soft rot in fleshy fruits.

q: Sclerotinia causes soft rot of ____.
e: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum causes watery soft rot in a wide variety of vegetable crops.

q: Not all bacteria are bad for plants and soil; in fact, most are ____.
e: The majority of soil bacteria play crucial beneficial roles in nutrient cycling and soil health.

q: There are approximately ____ types of bacteria that cause diseases in plants.
e: While most bacteria are harmless or beneficial, roughly 200 specific types are known plant pathogens.

q: Bacteria that cause plant diseases are most active in warm and ____ environments.
e: Bacterial pathogens thrive and multiply rapidly in conditions characterized by high warmth and humidity.

q: Most plant pathogenic bacteria belong to the following genera: Agrobacterium, Erwinia, Pseudomonas, Streptomyces and ____.
e: Xanthomonas is a widespread genus of bacteria responsible for numerous leaf spot and blight diseases.

q: Nematodes are simple, multicellular animals and are bilaterally symmetrical, soft-bodied, non-segmented ____.
e: Nematodes are anatomically classified as unsegmented, bilaterally symmetrical roundworms.

q: Most nematode species that attack plants are ____.
e: Plant-parasitic nematodes are generally too small to be seen with the naked eye, requiring microscopic examination.

q: Plant parasitic nematodes have a ____, a piercing mouthpart.
e: The stylet is a specialized, spear-like mouthpart used by plant-parasitic nematodes to pierce plant cells.

q: The presence of a stylet is the key diagnostic sign differentiating plant parasitic nematodes from all other types of ____.
e: The stylet is the defining morphological feature that separates plant-parasitic nematodes from free-living species.

q: Root-knot nematodes belong to the genus ____.
e: Meloidogyne is the genus of nematodes responsible for forming characteristic galls or knots on plant roots.

q: Plant diseases caused by infectious pathogens have seriously affected human society and nature through their damages to food production, ____ development.
e: Crop losses due to plant diseases have profound negative impacts on global economic development and food security.

q: To prevent, mitigate or control plant diseases, different approaches can be used: biological, physical and ____.
e: The three primary pillars of plant disease management are biological, physical, and chemical control methods.

q: Biological control is control of plant diseases using living ____.
e: Biological control relies on introducing or encouraging living microorganisms that antagonize plant pathogens.

q: Four main mechanisms involved in the biocontrol are (i) the biological agent (antagonist) may parasite the other organism, (ii) antagonist may secrete metabolites (antibiotics) harmful to the pathogens (____), (iii) antagonist may compete with the pathogens for nutrients or space (competition) and (iv) may cause death of the parasite by producing enzymes (lysis).
e: Antibiosis occurs when a biocontrol agent produces chemical metabolites that inhibit or kill the target pathogen.

q: Physical methods of disease prevention are based on the physiological ____ of disease agents to adverse conditions.
e: Physical control exploits the limits of a pathogen's physiological tolerance to extreme temperatures or moisture deprivation.

q: Physical control involves the removal of pathogen sources or presence of physical ____ to prevent contact between the disease agent and the host.
e: Physical barriers, such as mulches or nets, physically block pathogens or vectors from reaching the host plant.

q: Chemicals used to control bacteria (____), fungi (fungicides), and nematodes (nematicides) may be applied to seeds, foliage, flowers, fruit, or soil.
e: Bactericides are specific chemical agents formulated to kill or inhibit the growth of plant-pathogenic bacteria.

q: Chemicals used to control fungi are known as ____.
e: Fungicides are widely used in agriculture to protect crops from destructive fungal infections.

q: Chemicals used to control nematodes are known as ____.
e: Nematicides are chemical treatments applied to soil to manage populations of plant-parasitic nematodes.

q: A disease is an illness or disorder of the body or mind that leads to poor ____.
e: Diseases are characterized by a decline in the normal physiological or mental health of an organism.

q: All animals, including human, suffer from one kind of disease or another during their ____.
e: Exposure to pathogens and environmental factors ensures that all animals encounter disease during their lifespan.

q: Animal diseases can be divided into non-infectious diseases and ____ diseases.
e: Animal diseases are broadly categorized based on whether they are caused by transmissible pathogens or non-living factors.

q: Non-infectious diseases are those that are not caused by ____, so that they cannot spread from one person to another.
e: Because they lack a biological pathogen, non-infectious diseases are not communicable between individuals.

q: Non-infectious diseases are caused by factors such as aging, genetics, malnutrition, lifestyle and ____.
e: Environmental factors, combined with genetics and lifestyle, play a major role in the development of non-infectious diseases.

q: Examples of non-infectious diseases include cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, diabetes, and ____.
e: Alzheimer's is a progressive neurological disorder classified as a non-infectious disease.

q: Most cardiovascular disease starts with ____ formation.
e: The foundational step in most cardiovascular diseases is the accumulation of atheromas within arterial walls.

q: If the ____, the inner lining of the wall of the artery, is damaged by high blood pressure, an inflammatory response where by white blood cells (mostly macrophages) move into the area.
e: Damage to the endothelium initiates the inflammatory cascade that leads to plaque buildup in arteries.

q: White blood cells (mostly macrophages) and lipids from the blood clump together under the endothelium to form fatty ____.
e: Fatty streaks are the earliest visible lesions in the development of atherosclerosis.

q: Over time, more white blood cells, lipids and connective tissue build up and harden to form a fibrous plaque called ____.
e: An atheroma is a hardened, fibrous plaque that narrows the arterial lumen and restricts blood flow.

q: This plaque partially blocks the ____ of the artery and restricts blood flow.
e: The lumen is the inner open space of an artery, which becomes narrowed by the growth of an atheroma.

q: The hardening of arteries, caused by atheroma, is called ____.
e: Atherosclerosis is the specific medical term for the hardening and narrowing of arteries due to plaque buildup.

q: In angina, plaques build up slowly in the ____ arteries, reducing blood flow to the parts of the heart muscle.
e: The coronary arteries are responsible for supplying oxygenated blood directly to the heart muscle.

q: Often symptoms of angina are first noticed during ____, when the cardiac muscle is working harder and needs more oxygen.
e: Physical exertion increases the heart's oxygen demand, triggering angina pain if coronary arteries are narrowed.

q: The narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough oxygenated blood and the heart muscle resorts to ____ respiration.
e: When oxygen supply is insufficient, heart muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid and causing pain.

q: The symptoms of angina subside once exercise ____.
e: Resting reduces the heart's oxygen demand, allowing angina symptoms to subside.

q: Oxygen is supplied to the heart muscle by the ____ arteries.
e: Blockages in the coronary arteries directly deprive the heart muscle of vital oxygen.

q: If the coronary artery becomes completely blocked by a blood clot, an area of the heart muscle will be totally cut off from its blood supply, causing myocardial ____.
e: Myocardial infarction is the medical term for tissue death in the heart muscle due to a complete lack of blood flow.

q: Myocardial infarction is more commonly known as a heart ____.
e: A heart attack occurs when blood flow to a part of the heart is severely restricted or blocked.

q: A stroke is caused by an interruption to the normal blood supply to an area of the ____.
e: Strokes occur when blood flow to the brain is disrupted, leading to rapid neurological damage.

q: A blockage in the brain is usually caused by a blood clot, an atheroma or a combination of the ____.
e: Thrombotic strokes often involve a combination of a pre-existing atheroma and a newly formed blood clot.

q: Very often in a stroke, the blood is cut off from one part or one ____ of the brain only.
e: Strokes frequently affect only one hemisphere or side of the brain, leading to unilateral symptoms.

q: In more severe strokes, there can be ____, usually on one side of the body.
e: Loss of motor function, or paralysis, is a common and severe consequence of brain tissue damage during a stroke.

q: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot in a vein ____ inside the body.
e: DVT specifically refers to clot formation in the deep venous system, rather than superficial veins.

q: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) usually happens in ____ veins.
e: The deep veins of the lower extremities (legs) are the most common sites for DVT formation.

q: DVT can be caused by prolong inactivity such as during long-haul ____.
e: Prolonged sitting and immobility during long flights significantly increase the risk of developing DVT.

q: The three main risk factors for CVDs which cannot be changed are genes, age, and ____.
e: Gender is a non-modifiable risk factor, with males generally facing a higher baseline risk for cardiovascular diseases.

q: As a person gets older, the blood vessels begin to lose their ____ and to narrow slightly.
e: The natural aging process causes arterial walls to stiffen and lose their normal elasticity.

q: Men are more likely to suffer from heart disease (and other CVDs) than ____.
e: Statistically, men have a higher incidence of cardiovascular diseases compared to women, especially at younger ages.

q: Substances in tobacco smoke can damage the artery ____, which makes the build-up of plaques more likely.
e: Chemicals in tobacco smoke directly injure the endothelial linings of arteries, initiating plaque formation.

q: Smoking also changes the balance of ____ in the blood.
e: Smoking negatively alters blood lipid profiles, typically lowering HDL and raising LDL cholesterol levels.

q: Sedentary lifestyle can lead to heart diseases, obesity, high blood pressure and ____.
e: Physical inactivity is a major modifiable risk factor that contributes to the development of type 2 diabetes and CVDs.

q: A healthy blood pressure is around ____ mmHg during systole and around80 mmHg during diastole.
e: A normal systolic blood pressure reading is approximately 120 mmHg.

q: If the blood pressure is regularly above 140/90 mmHg, it is a sign of high blood pressure or ____.
e: Hypertension is the clinical diagnosis for chronically elevated blood pressure, a major risk factor for CVDs.

q: Most scientists think that the best predictors of future CVDs are where fat is stored on the body, how much exercise a person does and the levels of different ____ in the blood.
e: Blood lipid profiles, including cholesterol and triglycerides, are critical indicators of cardiovascular risk.

q: Type 2 diabetes can result in damage to the lining of the blood vessels which increases the risk of ____ formation.
e: Chronically high blood sugar in diabetes damages blood vessels and accelerates atherosclerotic plaque formation.

q: Eating a balanced diet with a variety of fats and plenty of fruit and ____ helps prevent atherosclerosis.
e: A diet rich in fruits and vegetables provides antioxidants and fiber that protect cardiovascular health.

q: Not smoking and maintaining a healthy ____- a body mass index (BMI) of 18.5- 25 kgm is the ideal range.
e: Maintaining a healthy body weight, as measured by BMI, is crucial for reducing cardiovascular strain.

q: Taking regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle and helps to control blood pressure and ____ level.
e: Regular aerobic exercise is highly effective at lowering blood pressure and improving cholesterol profiles.

q: Antihypertensives drugs such as beta blockers, sympathetic nerve inhibitors, ACE inhibitors are prescribed to reduce blood ____.
e: Antihypertensive medications are specifically designed to lower systemic blood pressure and reduce cardiac workload.

q: To lower the level of cholesterol in the blood, a group of drugs known as ____ is used.
e: Statins are the primary class of medications used to inhibit cholesterol synthesis in the liver.

q: Statins improve the balance of LDLs (low-density lipoprotein) to ____ (high-density lipoprotein).
e: HDLs are considered 'good' cholesterol, and improving the LDL to HDL ratio reduces atherosclerosis risk.

q: Plant stanols and sterols compounds are now widely sold in spreads and ____, which also reduce the levels of LDLs in the blood.
e: Foods fortified with plant stanols and sterols, like certain yoghurts, can help block cholesterol absorption in the gut.

q: Anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin and heparin) are a class of medicines used to reduce blood ____.
e: Anticoagulants prevent the coagulation cascade, reducing the risk of dangerous blood clots forming.

q: Platelet inhibitory drugs such as ____ are also a type of anticoagulant.
e: Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation, serving as a common preventative treatment against arterial thrombosis.

q: Infectious diseases are diseases that are caused by organisms known as ____.
e: Pathogens are the specific biological agents, such as bacteria or viruses, that cause infectious diseases.

q: Infectious diseases are sometimes called ____ diseases as they are passed from infected to uninfected people.
e: The term communicable highlights the ability of these diseases to be transmitted between hosts.

q: The way in which a pathogen passes from one host to another is called the transmission ____.
e: The transmission cycle describes the complete pathway and mechanisms by which a pathogen moves between hosts.

q: The ____ of a disease is the number of people who have that disease at any one time.
e: Prevalence measures the total existing cases of a disease in a population at a specific point in time.

q: Diseases that are always in populations are described as ____.
e: An endemic disease maintains a constant, baseline presence within a specific geographic area or population.

q: An ____ occurs when there is a sudden increase in the number of people with a disease.
e: An epidemic represents a rapid, widespread outbreak of disease that exceeds normal endemic expectations.

q: A ____ occurs when there is an increase in the number of cases throughout a continent or across the world.
e: A pandemic is a global epidemic, affecting vast geographical regions and international populations.

q: The death rate from different diseases is referred to as ____.
e: Mortality rates quantify the frequency of deaths within a population due to a specific disease.

q: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio ____.
e: Vibrio cholerae is the waterborne bacterium responsible for the severe diarrheal disease cholera.

q: Malaria is caused by four species of ____.
e: Plasmodium is the genus of parasitic protists that cause malaria in humans.

q: HIV/AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, which is a type of ____.
e: HIV is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, leading to AIDS.

q: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. ____.
e: Mycobacterium bovis is a related bacterial species that can also cause tuberculosis, often transmitted from cattle.

q: Most cases of malaria are caused by one of four species of the protist ____.
e: The Plasmodium protist has a complex life cycle involving both human and mosquito hosts.

q: The method of transmission for malaria is an insect vector: the female ____ mosquito.
e: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria, as they require blood meals for egg development.

q: Malaria is endemic in ____ countries globally.
e: Malaria remains a significant endemic health burden in over 100 tropical and subtropical countries.

q: The incubation period for malaria is from a week to a ____.
e: Depending on the Plasmodium species, malaria symptoms can take up to a year to manifest after infection.

q: The site of action of the malaria pathogen includes the liver, red blood cells, and ____.
e: Severe malaria, particularly caused by P. falciparum, can infect brain capillaries, leading to cerebral malaria.

q: Clinical features of malaria include fever, anaemia, nausea, headaches, muscle pain, shivering, sweating, and enlarged ____.
e: The spleen enlarges (splenomegaly) as it works overtime to clear infected red blood cells from circulation.

q: Malaria can be diagnosed by microscopical examination of blood or a dip stick test for malaria ____ in blood.
e: Rapid diagnostic tests (dip sticks) detect specific Plasmodium antigens circulating in the patient's blood.

q: In 2012, there were about 207 million cases of malaria worldwide, with about 80% in ____.
e: The African continent bears the disproportionately highest global burden of malaria cases and mortality.

q: Female Anopheles mosquitoes feed on human blood to obtain the ____ they need to develop their eggs.
e: The protein derived from a blood meal is essential for the maturation of mosquito eggs.

q: Male and female gametes fuse in the mosquito's ____ and develop to form infective stages.
e: Sexual reproduction of the Plasmodium parasite occurs within the midgut of the Anopheles mosquito.

q: When the mosquito feeds again, it injects an ____ from its salivary glands that prevents the blood meal from clotting.
e: Mosquito saliva contains anticoagulants that keep blood flowing, which simultaneously introduces the malaria parasite.

q: The parasites enter the red blood cells, where they ____.
e: Asexual reproduction and massive multiplication of Plasmodium occur inside human red blood cells.

q: Malaria may also be transmitted during blood ____ and when unsterile needles are re-used.
e: Because the parasite resides in red blood cells, it can be transmitted via contaminated blood transfusions.

q: Plasmodium can also pass across the ____ from mother to fetus.
e: Congenital malaria can occur if the parasite crosses the placental barrier during pregnancy.

q: If people are continually re-infected by different strains of malaria they become ____.
e: Continuous exposure to endemic malaria eventually leads to acquired, albeit partial, immunity in adults.

q: Immunity to malaria only lasts as long as people are in ____ with the disease.
e: Malaria immunity is not lifelong; it wanes rapidly if a person leaves the endemic area and loses regular contact with the parasite.

q: Quinine and chloroquine are anti-malarial drugs used to treat infected people and as ____ drugs.
e: Prophylactic drugs are taken preventatively to stop the malaria parasite from establishing an infection.

q: Chloroquine inhibits protein synthesis and prevents the parasite ____ within the body.
e: By halting protein synthesis, chloroquine stops the parasite from multiplying and spreading through the bloodstream.

q: Proguanil has the added advantage of inhibiting the sexual ____ of Plasmodium inside the biting mosquito.
e: Proguanil disrupts the parasite's life cycle by preventing its sexual reproduction phase within the mosquito vector.

q: Where anti-malarial drugs have been used widely, there are strains of drug-resistant ____.
e: Heavy reliance on specific anti-malarials has driven the evolutionary selection for drug-resistant Plasmodium strains.

q: Mefloquine is a new drug used in South America, Africa and New ____.
e: Mefloquine is deployed in regions with known chloroquine resistance, such as parts of South America, Africa, and New Guinea.

q: Artesunate, a drug derived from the plant compound ____, is used in combination with mefloquine to treat infections of P. falciparum.
e: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are currently the most effective treatment for P. falciparum malaria.

q: There are three main ways to control malaria: reduce the number of mosquitoes, avoid being bitten, and use ____ to prevent the parasite infecting people.
e: Chemoprophylaxis (using drugs) is a critical pillar of malaria control alongside vector management.

q: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in ____.
e: Stagnant water provides the necessary aquatic environment for mosquito eggs to hatch and larvae to develop.

q: Oil can be spread over the surfaces of water to make it impossible for mosquito larvae and pupae to ____.
e: A surface oil film blocks the breathing siphons of aquatic mosquito larvae, causing them to suffocate.

q: Stocking ponds with fish which feed on mosquito larvae, e.g., mosquito fish Gambusia ____.
e: Gambusia affinis is a biological control agent widely used to consume mosquito larvae in standing water.

q: Spraying a preparation containing the bacterium Bacillus ____, which kills mosquito larvae but is not toxic to other forms of life.
e: Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) produces toxins specific to mosquito larvae, making it a safe biological insecticide.

q: The best protection against malaria is to avoid being ____.
e: Preventing mosquito bites is the most direct and effective way to avoid malaria transmission.

q: People are advised to sleep beneath mosquito ____ and use insect repellents.
e: Insecticide-treated bed nets provide a crucial physical and chemical barrier against night-biting Anopheles mosquitoes.

q: Soaking mosquito nets in insecticide every ____ months has been shown to reduce mortality from malaria.
e: Regular re-treatment of nets every six months ensures the insecticide remains potent and effective.

q: In the 1950s, the World Health Organization (WHO) coordinated a worldwide ____ programme.
e: The WHO launched an ambitious global malaria eradication campaign in the mid-20th century.

q: The WHO eradication programme was not generally successful because Plasmodium became resistant to the ____ used to control it.
e: The emergence of drug-resistant parasites severely undermined early global malaria eradication efforts.

q: Mosquitoes became resistant to dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane (____) and the other insecticides that were used at the time.
e: Widespread use of DDT led to rapid evolutionary resistance in mosquito populations, halting vector control progress.

q: Between 2000 and 2011, control measures achieved a decrease in mortality rates of about 25% across the world, and 33% in the WHO's ____ region.
e: Targeted interventions in the African region yielded significant reductions in malaria-related mortality during that decade.

q: The introduction of simple dip stick tests for diagnosing malaria means that diagnosis can be done quickly without the need for ____.
e: Rapid diagnostic tests allow for immediate, field-based diagnosis without requiring complex laboratory microscopy.

q: The whole genome of Plasmodium has been ____, and this may lead to the development of effective vaccines.
e: Mapping the complete genetic sequence of Plasmodium provides vital targets for modern vaccine research.

q: Drugs are used in ____ to reduce the chances of drug resistance arising.
e: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) use multiple drugs simultaneously to prevent the parasite from developing resistance.
